source.name: ASTRA chemistry practice set
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: Electrical conductance of a solution is defined as the
options: product of resistance and cell constant
questions.explanation: Conductance $G = 1/R$. A smaller resistance means the solution conducts more readily.

questions.stem: The SI unit used for electrical conductance is the
questions.explanation: Siemens is the reciprocal ohm. Older texts also write mho for the same unit.

questions.stem: Specific conductivity $\kappa$ of an electrolyte solution is the conductance of
options: a unit cube of the solution between opposite faces
one mole of solute placed between inert plates
a metallic wire of the same length
questions.explanation: $\kappa$ is intensive: it is $G$ measured for unit length and unit cross-section of solution.

questions.stem: The cell constant of a conductivity cell equals
options: distance between electrodes divided by electrode area
electrode area divided by distance between electrodes
questions.explanation: Cell constant $= \ell/A$. It converts the measured conductance into specific conductivity.

questions.stem: Specific conductivity is obtained from the measured conductance $G$ by writing
questions.explanation: Because $G = \kappa A/\ell$, rearranging gives $\kappa = G \times$ cell constant.

questions.stem: Molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is related to specific conductivity and molar concentration $c$ by
questions.explanation: In SI, $\Lambda_m = \kappa/c$. In older cgs usage one writes $\Lambda_m = 1000\,\kappa/M$ with $M$ in mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: As an aqueous electrolyte is made more dilute, its specific conductivity $\kappa$ generally
options: falls because fewer ions occupy each cubic centimetre
rises because every ion becomes heavier
stays fixed at the value of pure water
questions.explanation: Dilution lowers the number of charge carriers per unit volume, so $\kappa$ decreases even though ions may move more freely.

questions.stem: The usual laboratory unit of cell constant is
questions.explanation: $\ell/A$ has dimensions of inverse length, so cm$^{-1}$ or m$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: For a strong electrolyte such as KCl, further dilution produces
options: only a modest further rise in $\Lambda_m$
a sudden drop of $\Lambda_m$ to zero
a collapse of $\kappa$ to a negative value
questions.explanation: Strong electrolytes are already fully ionised; $\Lambda_m$ creeps up mainly because interionic drag weakens.

questions.stem: Metallic conduction differs from electrolytic conduction in that metals carry current by
options: mobile electrons, without chemical change of the conductor
migration of cations and anions that are discharged at electrodes
protons hopping through a salt bridge only
neutral solvent molecules drifting in the field
questions.explanation: A metal conducts via its electron gas. An electrolyte conducts by ion movement and is chemically changed at the electrodes.

questions.stem: A conductivity cell of constant $1.5\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ reads $G = 0.020\ \mathrm{S}$ for a solution. The specific conductivity is
questions.explanation: $\kappa = G \times (\ell/A) = 0.020 \times 1.5 = 0.030\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: If $\kappa = 0.0050\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}$ for a $0.020\ \mathrm{M}$ solution, $\Lambda_m$ in S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$ equals
A 0.10 M KCl standard with $\kappa = 0.0129\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}$ shows $R = 86\ \Omega$ in a cell. The cell constant is nearest
questions.explanation: $G = 1/86\ \mathrm{S}$, so $\ell/A = \kappa/G = 0.0129 \times 86 \approx 1.11\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: Comparing $\kappa$ and $\Lambda_m$ as a strong electrolyte is diluted, the typical pattern is that
questions.explanation: Fewer ions per cm$^3$ lower $\kappa$, but each mole of electrolyte contributes more free ionic mobility, so $\Lambda_m$ rises.

questions.stem: The slight increase of $\Lambda_m$ of NaCl on dilution is attributed mainly to
options: weaker interionic attractions, so ions migrate faster
fresh ionisation of previously undissociated NaCl molecules
a change in the Faraday constant
conversion of NaCl into a weak electrolyte
questions.explanation: NaCl is already fully dissociated. Dilution reduces ion-atmosphere drag (Debye–Hückel–Onsager), raising molar conductivity a little.

questions.stem: A 0.050 M solution in a cell of constant $1.20\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ has $R = 50\ \Omega$. $\Lambda_m$ of the solute is
Kohlrausch's law of independent migration states that $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of an electrolyte is
options: the sum of the limiting ionic conductivities of its cation and anion
independent of the identities of the two ions
measurable only for metals, not for salts
questions.explanation: At infinite dilution each ion migrates independently, so $\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+\lambda_+^\circ + \nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$.

questions.stem: For a 1:1 salt MX the limiting molar conductivity may be written
questions.explanation: One mole of MX yields one mole of each ion, so the ionic contributions simply add.

questions.stem: Limiting molar conductivity of a weak electrolyte such as ethanoic acid is obtained by
options: combining $\Lambda_m^\circ$ values of suitable strong electrolytes, not by plotting $\Lambda_m$ versus $\sqrt{c}$
extrapolating a Kohlrausch $\sqrt{c}$ graph of the weak acid itself
questions.explanation: A weak acid is far from fully ionised even when dilute, so the $\sqrt{c}$ plot does not give a reliable intercept.

questions.stem: Degree of dissociation of a weak electrolyte is estimated from conductivities as
questions.explanation: At a given concentration the fraction ionised is the ratio of the observed molar conductivity to the infinite-dilution value.

questions.stem: A practical use of Kohlrausch's law is the evaluation of
options: $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of a poorly conducting weak acid from data on strong salts and acids
the Faraday constant from a copper voltameter
the order of a homogeneous reaction
questions.explanation: Typical combination: $\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}) + \Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{HCl}) - \Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{NaCl})$.

questions.stem: Limiting molar conductivity $\Lambda_m^\circ$ refers to the molar conductivity
options: extrapolated to infinite dilution, where ions no longer hinder one another
of the solid crystal before it dissolves
at the boiling point of the solvent only
questions.explanation: Infinite dilution removes ion–ion interactions, so each ion contributes its characteristic $\lambda^\circ$.

questions.stem: Among common aqueous ions, the unusually large $\lambda^\circ$ belongs to
options: $\mathrm{Li}^+$ only, because it is the lightest metal ion
questions.explanation: Grotthuss proton/hydroxide hopping through the hydrogen-bond network gives $\mathrm{H}^+$ and $\mathrm{OH}^-$ exceptional mobility.

questions.stem: Given $\Lambda_m^\circ/\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$ of CH$_3$COONa = 91, HCl = 426 and NaCl = 126, $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of CH$_3$COOH is
questions.explanation: $\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{HOAc}) = 91 + 426 - 126 = 391\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$ by Kohlrausch combination.

questions.stem: A weak acid has $\Lambda_m = 16\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$ and $\Lambda_m^\circ = 400\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$. Its degree of dissociation is
questions.explanation: $\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda_m^\circ = 16/400 = 0.040$.

questions.stem: Which set of limiting molar conductivities yields $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of NH$_4$OH?
questions.explanation: Adding NH$_4$Cl and NaOH supplies NH$_4^+$ and OH$^-$; subtracting NaCl removes the spectator Na$^+$ and Cl$^-$.

questions.stem: For a weak monobasic acid, $K_a$ is related to the conductivity ratio $\alpha$ and the molarity $c$ by
questions.explanation: Ostwald dilution: $K_a = \alpha^2 c /(1-\alpha) \approx \alpha^2 c$ when $\alpha \ll 1$.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid at $0.010\ \mathrm{M}$ has $\Lambda_m = 16.0$ and $\Lambda_m^\circ = 390\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$. $K_a$ is nearest
questions.explanation: $\alpha = 16/390 \approx 0.041$; then $K_a \approx \alpha^2 c = (0.041)^2 \times 0.010 \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-5}$.

questions.stem: A galvanic (voltaic) cell is a device that
options: converts chemical energy of a spontaneous redox change into electrical energy
uses an external battery to force a non-spontaneous reaction
stores charge on two metal plates like a capacitor
measures conductance of an electrolyte only
questions.explanation: In a galvanic cell a spontaneous cell reaction drives electrons through an external circuit.

questions.stem: Inside a working galvanic cell, the cathode is the electrode at which
options: reduction of the oxidant takes place
questions.explanation: By definition the cathode is the reduction site. In a galvanic cell it is the positive terminal.

questions.stem: The salt bridge in a galvanic cell is provided mainly to
options: maintain electrical neutrality in the two half-cells
supply the electrons that travel in the wire
keep the two metals from touching the solution
questions.explanation: Ions from the bridge migrate to cancel charge build-up so the cell can continue to operate.

questions.stem: The standard hydrogen electrode is assigned, by convention, an $E^\circ$ of
questions.explanation: SHE ($a_{\mathrm{H}^+} = 1$, $p_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}$) is the reference zero of the $E^\circ$ scale.

questions.stem: Standard cell EMF is obtained from standard reduction potentials as
questions.explanation: Equivalently $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}} = E^\circ_{\mathrm{red}}(\mathrm{oxidant}) + E^\circ_{\mathrm{ox}}(\mathrm{reductant})$.

questions.stem: In standard cell notation the electrode written on the left is the
questions.explanation: The IUPAC line diagram is anode | anodic electrolyte || cathodic electrolyte | cathode.

questions.stem: The line diagram of the Daniell cell is customarily written
questions.explanation: Zinc is oxidised (left) and Cu$^{2+}$ is reduced on copper (right).

questions.stem: A positive value of $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}}$ means that, under standard conditions, the cell reaction is
questions.explanation: $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$; a positive $E^\circ$ makes $\Delta G^\circ$ negative, so the written reaction proceeds spontaneously.

questions.stem: In the external metallic circuit of a galvanic cell, electrons travel
options: from the anode toward the cathode
from the cathode toward the anode
through the salt bridge as free electrons
in both directions at equal speed
questions.explanation: Oxidation releases electrons at the anode; they flow through the wire to the cathode, where reduction consumes them.

questions.stem: Standard electrode potential is an intensive quantity, so doubling the size of a half-cell
questions.explanation: Potential does not scale with the amount of electrode or electrolyte, unlike extensive $\Delta G$.

questions.stem: Among several half-cells, the strongest oxidising agent is the couple with the
options: largest number of electrons in the half-reaction
questions.explanation: A large positive $E^\circ$ means the oxidised form is readily reduced, i.e. it is a strong oxidant.

questions.stem: A gas electrode such as the hydrogen electrode employs platinum chiefly as
options: an inert surface on which the redox couple can exchange electrons
the species that is oxidised in place of hydrogen
questions.explanation: Pt is chemically inert here; it provides a conducting surface for $\mathrm{H^+} / \mathrm{H_2}$.

questions.stem: The EMF of a cell is the potential difference measured when
options: a very large current is forced through the cell
the cell is short-circuited with a copper wire
questions.explanation: EMF is the reversible, zero-current voltage. A working current produces an IR drop, so the measured voltage is smaller.

questions.stem: If $E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}) = +0.34\ \mathrm{V}$ and $E^\circ(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}) = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}$, $E^\circ$ of the Daniell cell is
questions.explanation: $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10\ \mathrm{V}$.

questions.stem: For the couples $\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}$ ($E^\circ = +0.80\ \mathrm{V}$) and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}$ ($E^\circ = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}$), the anode of the spontaneous cell is
questions.explanation: The more negative couple is oxidised: Zn dissolves at the anode while Ag$^+$ is reduced.

questions.stem: The strongest reducing agent among Zn, Cu, Ag and H$_2$ (use $E^\circ$: Zn $-0.76$, H $0.00$, Cu $+0.34$, Ag $+0.80\ \mathrm{V}$) is
questions.explanation: The most negative reduction potential belongs to Zn$^{2+}$/Zn, so metallic zinc is the strongest reductant of the set.

questions.stem: The standard Gibbs energy change of a cell reaction is related to $E^\circ$ by
questions.explanation: Electrical work available from a reversible cell is $nFE$; that work equals $-\Delta G$.

questions.stem: The notation $\mathrm{Pt}|\mathrm{Fe^{2+},Fe^{3+}}||\mathrm{Ag^+}|\mathrm{Ag}$ implies that the cell reaction is
questions.explanation: Left-hand side is oxidised (Fe$^{2+} \to$ Fe$^{3+}$) and right-hand side is reduced (Ag$^+ \to$ Ag).

questions.stem: In an electrolytic cell, as opposed to a galvanic cell, the anode is
options: the positive electrode, still the site of oxidation
the negative electrode, the site of reduction
unnecessary if a salt bridge is present
questions.explanation: Oxidation is always anodic. An external source makes the electrolytic anode positive, whereas a galvanic anode is negative.

questions.stem: A large positive $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}}$ corresponds to
options: a large equilibrium constant for the cell reaction
questions.explanation: $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -nFE^\circ$, so a sizable positive $E^\circ$ means $K \gg 1$.

questions.stem: For Zn–Cu with $E^\circ = 1.10\ \mathrm{V}$ and $n = 2$, $\Delta G^\circ$ is nearest ($F = 96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}$)
questions.explanation: $\Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96500 \times 1.10 = -212300\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} \approx -212\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: Couples: $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}/Ni} = -0.25\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag} = +0.80\ \mathrm{V}$. The spontaneous standard cell and its $E^\circ$ are
questions.explanation: Ni is the better reductant, so it is the anode. $E^\circ = 0.80 - (-0.25) = 1.05\ \mathrm{V}$.

questions.stem: The Nernst equation for a cell reaction with reaction quotient $Q$ is
questions.explanation: The correction term subtracts a quantity that grows with $Q$, so the cell voltage falls as products accumulate.

questions.stem: At $298\ \mathrm{K}$ the Nernst factor $2.303RT/F$ is close to
questions.explanation: Intermediate problems therefore write $E = E^\circ - (0.059/n)\log Q$ at 25 °C.

questions.stem: When every species in the cell reaction is in its standard state, $Q = 1$ and therefore
questions.explanation: The log term vanishes at $Q = 1$, recovering the standard EMF.

questions.stem: A concentration cell that uses the same couple on both sides has
options: $E^\circ = 0$, but a non-zero $E$ if the two concentrations differ
$E^\circ$ equal to twice a single-electrode potential
no possible EMF under any condition
questions.explanation: The two standard potentials cancel. The remaining voltage comes only from the concentration (activity) ratio.

questions.stem: As the reaction quotient $Q$ of a galvanic cell increases, the cell EMF generally
questions.explanation: $E = E^\circ - (RT/nF)\ln Q$, so a larger $Q$ reduces $E$. At equilibrium $Q = K$ and $E = 0$.

questions.stem: For the half-cell $\mathrm{M}^{n+} + n\,e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{M}(s)$, the Nernst expression at 298 K is
questions.explanation: Solid metal has activity 1, so $Q = 1/[\mathrm{M}^{n+}]$ and the sign of the log term flips.

questions.stem: The integer $n$ that appears in the Nernst equation is the
options: number of moles of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction
number of ions in the salt bridge
atomic number of the anode metal
questions.explanation: $n$ comes from the balanced redox equation (for Daniell, $n = 2$).

questions.stem: When a galvanic cell has run down to equilibrium, the Nernst voltage satisfies
questions.explanation: No further driving force remains ($E = 0$), which forces $Q$ to equal the equilibrium constant $K$.

questions.stem: The potential of a hydrogen electrode at 298 K, $p_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}$, varies with pH as
questions.explanation: $E = 0.059\log[\mathrm{H}^+] = -0.059\,\mathrm{pH}$ when hydrogen is at unit pressure.

questions.stem: Raising the concentration of a product ion in the cell reaction, other terms fixed, will
options: reverse the definition of the anode
questions.explanation: Products appear in the numerator of $Q$. A larger $Q$ makes $(RT/nF)\ln Q$ larger and $E$ smaller.

questions.stem: Absolute temperature enters the Nernst equation because
options: the $RT/nF$ prefactor, and therefore the size of the $\log Q$ correction, depends on $T$
Faraday's constant itself is proportional to $T$
standard potentials are defined only at 0 K
questions.explanation: At higher $T$ a given $Q$ shifts $E$ farther from $E^\circ$. $E^\circ$ itself may also change with $T$, but that is a separate effect.

questions.stem: A Daniell cell with $E^\circ = 1.10\ \mathrm{V}$ has $[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}] = 0.10\ \mathrm{M}$ and $[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}] = 1.0\ \mathrm{M}$. $E$ at 298 K is nearest
For $\mathrm{Cu}|\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(0.010\ \mathrm{M})||\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(1.0\ \mathrm{M})|\mathrm{Cu}$ at 298 K the EMF is
Take $E^\circ(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}/Zn}) = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}$. At $[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}] = 0.010\ \mathrm{M}$ and 298 K the zinc electrode potential is nearest
Starting from a standard Daniell cell, diluting only the Cu$^{2+}$ half-cell tenfold at 298 K changes $E$ by about
questions.explanation: $Q$ rises by 10, so $\Delta E = -(0.059/2)\log 10 \approx -0.030\ \mathrm{V}$.

questions.stem: A hydrogen electrode ($p_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}$) dipping into $0.0010\ \mathrm{M}$ HCl at 298 K develops a potential of
For $\mathrm{Zn}|\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}(0.10\ \mathrm{M})||\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(0.0010\ \mathrm{M})|\mathrm{Cu}$ with $E^\circ = 1.10\ \mathrm{V}$, $E$ at 298 K is
A Cu concentration cell shows $E = 0.0295\ \mathrm{V}$ at 298 K. The ratio $[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]_{\mathrm{cathode}}/[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]_{\mathrm{anode}}$ is
questions.explanation: $E = (0.059/2)\log(c_c/c_a) = 0.0295$ implies $\log(c_c/c_a) = 1$, so the concentration ratio is 10.

questions.stem: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass deposited is proportional to the
options: quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte
square of the applied voltage only
questions.explanation: $m = ZQ = ZIt$. Charge (current × time) fixes how much material is liberated.

questions.stem: Faraday's second law compares two electrolytes carrying the same charge and says the liberated masses are proportional to their
questions.explanation: Equal charge liberates equal numbers of equivalents, so $m_1/m_2 = E_1/E_2$.

questions.stem: One faraday of charge liberates from an electrolyte
options: exactly one gram of any metal
22.4 L of every gas at STP
questions.explanation: 1 F deposits 1 equivalent: 108 g Ag, 31.75 g Cu, 9 g Al, 11.2 L H$_2$ at STP, and so on.

questions.stem: The charge carried by one mole of electrons is called
questions.explanation: $F = N_A e \approx 96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}$. It is the charge needed to reduce one mole of a univalent ion.

questions.stem: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride yields, as the electrode products,
options: sodium metal at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode
hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
solid NaCl crystals on the anode
questions.explanation: In the melt the only ions are Na$^+$ and Cl$^-$, so Na and Cl$_2$ are discharged.

questions.stem: When aqueous CuSO$_4$ is electrolysed with copper electrodes, the anode reaction is
options: dissolution of copper metal as Cu$^{2+}$
questions.explanation: A copper anode is oxidised in preference to water or sulphate, so the anode loses mass while copper plates at the cathode.

questions.stem: Preferential discharge at an electrode is decided by
options: the ion that is most easily reduced (or oxidised) under the prevailing conditions
the ion present in the largest catalogue mass only
the cell constant of the vessel
questions.explanation: The couple with the more favourable discharge potential (including overvoltage and concentration) is liberated first.

questions.stem: The quantity of electricity $Q$ that flows in time $t$ at a steady current $I$ is
questions.explanation: Current is charge per unit time, so charge is the product $It$ (amperes × seconds = coulombs).

questions.stem: Electrolysis of acidified water with inert electrodes liberates
options: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, in a 2 : 1 volume ratio
oxygen at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
only hydrogen, because oxygen stays dissolved
questions.explanation: 2 H$_2$O → 2 H$_2$ + O$_2$. Two moles of hydrogen appear for each mole of oxygen.

questions.stem: During electrolysis the cathode is still defined as the electrode at which
options: the external battery is connected to earth
questions.explanation: The cathode/anode labels follow the chemistry (reduction/oxidation), not the galvanic sign convention.

questions.stem: Electrochemical equivalent $Z$ of a substance equals
questions.explanation: $m = ZQ$ with $Z = M/(nF)$, so $Z$ is the mass liberated by one coulomb.

questions.stem: To deposit one mole of aluminium from Al$^{3+}$ one must pass a charge of
questions.explanation: Each Al$^{3+}$ ion consumes three electrons, so 1 mol Al requires $3 \times 96500\ \mathrm{C}$.

questions.stem: A 1.0 A current sent for 965 s through aqueous AgNO$_3$ deposits silver (Ag = 108) amounting to
How many coulombs are required to plate 0.50 mol of copper from Cu$^{2+}$?
questions.explanation: Each mole of Cu$^{2+}$ needs 2 mol electrons, so 0.50 mol needs $1.0\,F = 96500\ \mathrm{C}$.

questions.stem: A 2.0 A current flows for 965 s through acidified water. The STP volume of H$_2$ evolved is nearest
questions.explanation: $Q = 1930\ \mathrm{C} = 0.020\ \mathrm{mol\ e^-}$; $2\,e^- \to 1\ \mathrm{H_2}$, so $0.010\ \mathrm{mol} = 0.224\ \mathrm{L}$ at STP.

questions.stem: To deposit 0.216 g of Ag (Ag = 108) from AgNO$_3$ at 0.50 A, the time required is
The same charge that deposits 1.08 g of silver will deposit, from Cu$^{2+}$ (Cu = 63.5), a copper mass of
questions.explanation: Equivalents: $E(\mathrm{Ag}) = 108$, $E(\mathrm{Cu}) = 31.75$. $m_{\mathrm{Cu}} = 1.08 \times 31.75/108 = 0.318\ \mathrm{g}$.

questions.stem: If 0.635 g of copper is plated from CuSO$_4$ in 1930 s, the steady current used was
A current of 2.0 A is passed for 30 min through molten Al$_2$O$_3$ (Al = 27). The mass of aluminium liberated is
questions.explanation: $Q = 2.0 \times 1800 = 3600\ \mathrm{C}$. $m = (27 \times 3600)/(3 \times 96500) \approx 0.336\ \mathrm{g}$.

questions.stem: The same current flows for the same time through AgNO$_3$ and then, separately, through AuCl$_3$ (Au = 197). If 1.08 g Ag is deposited, the gold deposited is nearest
questions.explanation: Equal charge means equal equivalents: $m_{\mathrm{Au}}/m_{\mathrm{Ag}} = (197/3)/108$, so $m_{\mathrm{Au}} = 1.08 \times 197/(3 \times 108) = 0.657\ \mathrm{g}$.

questions.stem: A primary electrochemical cell is one that
options: cannot be recharged by reversing the current
is recharged simply by plugging it into the mains
works only as an electrolytic cell
questions.explanation: Once the reductant and oxidant of a dry cell or button cell are spent, the cell is discarded.

questions.stem: A secondary cell differs from a primary cell in that it
options: can be recharged because the cell reaction is reversible
must be discarded after a single use
questions.explanation: Lead–acid and Ni–Cd cells are secondary batteries: charging drives the discharge reaction backwards.

questions.stem: The common dry cell (Leclanché) uses a zinc cup as the anode and, as the cathode depolariser,
options: manganese dioxide packed around a carbon rod
lead dioxide on a lead grid
questions.explanation: Zn is oxidised; MnO$_2$ is reduced at the carbon collector in the NH$_4$Cl / ZnCl$_2$ paste.

questions.stem: A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is designed so that the reactants are
options: fed continuously, and the cell can run as long as fuel and oxidant are supplied
sealed once and for all inside a closed can
the same as those of a lead storage battery
questions.explanation: A fuel cell is a galvanic cell with continuous feeds; it is not a store of a finite charge like a battery.

questions.stem: Rusting of iron is classified as an electrochemical process because it involves
options: local anodic oxidation of Fe and cathodic reduction of dissolved oxygen
a purely mechanical wearing away of the metal
photochemical cleavage of Fe–Fe bonds only
questions.explanation: Different surface spots act as tiny galvanic cells in the presence of a water film containing O$_2$.

questions.stem: Ordinary rusting of iron requires, besides the metal itself,
options: oxygen in a completely dry atmosphere only
solid NaCl with no water at all
questions.explanation: Water provides the ionic medium; oxygen is the cathodic oxidant. Dry iron in air rusts extremely slowly.

questions.stem: During discharge of a lead storage battery the electrolyte H$_2$SO$_4$ is consumed and the product deposited on both plates is
questions.explanation: Pb + PbO$_2$ + 2 H$_2$SO$_4$ → 2 PbSO$_4$ + 2 H$_2$O. Charging reverses this reaction and regenerates acid.

questions.stem: The only chemical product of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell operating with an alkaline or acid electrolyte is
questions.explanation: H$_2$ is oxidised and O$_2$ is reduced; their combination yields H$_2$O (and electrical work).

questions.stem: A buried iron pipeline is protected by attaching blocks of zinc or magnesium because those metals
options: act as sacrificial anodes and corrode in preference to iron
raise the $E^\circ$ of iron above that of oxygen
absorb all moisture from the soil
questions.explanation: Zn and Mg are more active (more negative $E^\circ$) than Fe, so they oxidise first and the pipeline becomes cathodic.

questions.stem: On a rusting iron surface the anodic half-change is Fe → Fe$^{2+}$ + 2 e$^-$. The matching cathodic process in a neutral water film is
questions.explanation: Dissolved oxygen is reduced to hydroxide. Fe$^{2+}$ and OH$^-$ then form rust (hydrated Fe$_2$O$_3$) after further oxidation.

questions.stem: The instantaneous rate of consumption of a reactant A is written
questions.explanation: Concentration of a reactant falls, so the minus sign makes the rate a positive quantity.

questions.stem: A rate law such as rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y$ must be established by
options: copying the stoichiometric coefficients in every case
the molecular mass of the product
questions.explanation: Orders $x$ and $y$ equal stoichiometric numbers only for an elementary step, not for an arbitrary overall equation.

questions.stem: The rate constant $k$ of a given reaction, at fixed temperature, does not depend on
options: the presence of a catalyst (which actually changes $k$)
questions.explanation: $k$ is independent of concentration. It does depend on $T$, $E_a$ and catalysis; the wording isolates the concentration independence.

questions.stem: Dimensions of $k$ for a zero-order reaction (rate in mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$) are
questions.explanation: Rate $= k$ when the order is zero, so $k$ carries the same units as the rate itself.

questions.stem: A second-order rate constant (concentration in mol L$^{-1}$, time in s) has the unit
questions.explanation: Rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^2$ (or $k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$) forces $k$ to have units (concentration)$^{-1}$ (time)$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: Average rate over a finite interval is computed as
options: change in concentration divided by the elapsed time
the slope of the tangent at one instant only
the equilibrium constant divided by time
questions.explanation: Average rate $= \Delta[\mathrm{ ]}/\Delta t$. Instantaneous rate is the derivative (tangent slope).

questions.stem: For $2\mathrm{N_2O_5} \to 4\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$, the rate of appearance of NO$_2$ compared with the rate of disappearance of N$_2$O$_5$ is
questions.explanation: Rate of reaction $= -\tfrac12 \mathrm{d}[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]/\mathrm{d}t = +\tfrac14 \mathrm{d}[\mathrm{NO_2}]/\mathrm{d}t$, so $-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]/\mathrm{d}t = \tfrac12 \mathrm{d}[\mathrm{NO_2}]/\mathrm{d}t$.

questions.stem: For an elementary bimolecular collision A + B → products, the rate law is expected to be
questions.explanation: In an elementary step the molecularity and the order coincide, so each reactant appears to the first power.

questions.stem: When a multi-step mechanism has one distinctly slow step, the observed rate law is usually that of the
options: rate-determining (slow) step, after any pre-equilibria are substituted
fastest step alone, ignoring the slow one
questions.explanation: The bottleneck step limits the flux. Intermediates in that step are rewritten using faster equilibria if needed.

questions.stem: Raising the temperature of a typical thermally activated reaction increases $k$ because
options: a larger fraction of collisions then exceeds the activation barrier
concentrations in the rate law are redefined
questions.explanation: Arrhenius behaviour: $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$ grows rapidly as $T$ rises.

questions.stem: The rate of the reaction $a\mathrm{A} \to$ products is defined so that
questions.explanation: Dividing by the stoichiometric coefficient makes the rate the same whichever species is monitored.

questions.stem: If rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^2$ and [A] is doubled at constant $T$, the instantaneous rate becomes
questions.explanation: Second order in A: $(2)^2 = 4$, so the rate quadruples.

questions.stem: A reaction has rate $= 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}$ when [A] = 0.10 M and is first order in A only. $k$ equals
questions.explanation: $k = \mathrm{rate}/[\mathrm{A}] = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}/0.10 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: For rate $= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$ the unit of $k$ (conc. in mol L$^{-1}$) is
questions.explanation: Two concentration factors sit with $k$, so $k$ is second-order: L mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: In $2\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \to \mathrm{C}$, if A disappears at $6.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}$, C appears at
questions.explanation: Rate $= -\tfrac12 \mathrm{d}[\mathrm{A}]/\mathrm{d}t = +\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{C}]/\mathrm{d}t$, so d[C]/dt is half of 6.0 × 10$^{-3}$.

questions.stem: Holding [B] fixed, [A] is doubled and the initial rate becomes four times larger. The order with respect to A is
questions.explanation: rate ∝ [A]$^x$ and $4 = 2^x$ implies $x = 2$.

questions.stem: Two runs at the same [B]: [A] = 0.10 M gives rate $1.2 \times 10^{-4}$; [A] = 0.20 M gives rate $4.8 \times 10^{-4}$. Order in A and the factor by which rate changes if both [A] and [B] are doubled (order in B is 1) are
questions.explanation: Rate ×4 when [A] ×2 ⇒ order 2 in A. Overall rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^2[\mathrm{B}]$, so doubling both species multiplies the rate by $4 \times 2 = 8$.

questions.stem: Rate $= k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{O_2}]$ with $k = 1.0 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{L^2\ mol^{-2}\ s^{-1}}$. If [NO] = 0.020 M and [O$_2$] = 0.010 M, the rate is
The order of a reaction may be zero or fractional, whereas molecularity is
options: a positive integer (1, 2 or occasionally 3) for an elementary step
allowed to be negative for unimolecular decays
questions.explanation: Order is experimental and can be 0, ½, 1, 2, …. Molecularity counts the molecules in one elementary act and is a small integer.

questions.stem: Molecularity of an elementary step is the
options: number of species that collide (or decompose) in that single step
sum of the stoichiometric coefficients of the overall equation always
same as the activation energy in kJ
questions.explanation: Unimolecular = one species rearranges; bimolecular = two species collide, and so on.

questions.stem: Overall order is obtained from a rate law rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y$ as
questions.explanation: Overall order is the sum of the concentration exponents in the experimental rate law.

questions.stem: A pseudo-first-order reaction is typically a bimolecular process run with
options: one reactant in large excess, so that its concentration stays nearly constant
both reactants at identical micromolar levels
a catalyst that raises the molecularity to four
questions.explanation: Ester hydrolysis in water is the classic case: [H$_2$O] is huge and is absorbed into an effective first-order $k$.

questions.stem: Molecularity is a meaningful idea only for
options: every complex multi-step reaction as a whole
questions.explanation: A complex reaction is a sequence of elementary steps; it has an order but not a single molecularity.

questions.stem: Decomposition of a single gaseous molecule in one elementary act is described as
questions.explanation: One reactant species appears in the elementary step, so the molecularity is one.

questions.stem: A bimolecular elementary reaction involves
options: a collision between two species (like or unlike)
the simultaneous meeting of four molecules
only a change of solvent polarity
questions.explanation: Two particles must encounter each other; the step is first order in each (or second order in one if they are identical).

questions.stem: Ammonia decomposition on a tungsten surface at high pressure is a familiar textbook example of a
options: unimolecular reaction in the gas phase only
questions.explanation: The surface is saturated, so the rate becomes independent of the NH$_3$ pressure: order zero.

questions.stem: The experimental law rate $= k[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{Br_2}]^{1/2}$ has overall order
questions.explanation: Exponents add: $1 + 1/2 = 3/2$.

questions.stem: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of methyl acetate in a large excess of water is treated as
options: pseudo first order in the ester
third order overall under all conditions
questions.explanation: [H$_2$O] is essentially constant, so the observed rate is first order in ester only.

questions.stem: For a reaction that proceeds by several elementary steps, the overall order
options: need not equal the molecularity of any one step, and is found only by experiment
is always equal to the number of steps
must equal the molecularity of the last step
is undefined if a catalyst is present
questions.explanation: Order is a property of the observed rate law. Molecularity belongs to individual steps.

questions.stem: Termolecular elementary steps are rare because
options: a simultaneous collision of three molecules is statistically improbable
three molecules can never share electrons
questions.explanation: Two-body collisions are common; a third body arriving in the same instant is unlikely, so $n = 3$ steps are scarce.

questions.stem: A rate constant reported as L$^2$ mol$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ indicates that the reaction is
questions.explanation: Units of $k$ are (conc.)$^{1-n}$ (time)$^{-1}$. L$^2$ mol$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ corresponds to $n = 3$.

questions.stem: Mechanism: fast equilibrium A + B ⇌ I, followed by slow I → P. The observed order in A and the molecularity of the slow step are
options: first order in A, and unimolecular
second order in A, and bimolecular
zero order in A, and termolecular
first order in A, and bimolecular
questions.explanation: The RDS is unimolecular in I. Substituting [I] = $K[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]$ makes the rate first order in A (and in B).

questions.stem: The integrated first-order rate law is commonly written
questions.explanation: Integration of $-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{A}]/\mathrm{d}t = k[\mathrm{A}]$ yields a linear plot of $\ln[\mathrm{A}]$ versus $t$.

questions.stem: For a zero-order decay the concentration falls linearly according to
questions.explanation: Rate $= k$ (constant), so [A] drops at a constant slope $-k$ until the reactant is exhausted.

questions.stem: The integrated law for a simple second-order reaction 2A → products is
questions.explanation: Integration of $-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{A}]/\mathrm{d}t = k[\mathrm{A}]^2$ produces the reciprocal-concentration relation.

questions.stem: A hallmark of first-order kinetics is that the half-life
options: does not depend on the starting concentration
questions.explanation: $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$ contains no $[\mathrm{A}]_0$. Each successive half-life has the same duration.

questions.stem: Zero-order half-life grows when the initial concentration is raised because
questions.explanation: A constant rate needs longer to consume half of a larger starting amount.

questions.stem: For the second-order process 2A → products, half-life and initial concentration are related by
questions.explanation: Set [A] = [A]$_0$/2 in $1/[\mathrm{A}] - 1/[\mathrm{A}]_0 = kt$ to obtain $t_{1/2} = 1/(k[\mathrm{A}]_0)$.

questions.stem: After $n$ successive half-lives of a first-order reaction the fraction of reactant left is
questions.explanation: Each half-life halves what remains, so the leftover fraction is $2^{-n}$.

questions.stem: A straight line is obtained when $\ln[\mathrm{A}]$ is plotted against time for a reaction that is
questions.explanation: The first-order integrated law is $\ln[\mathrm{A}] = \ln[\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$.

questions.stem: A plot of [A] versus time is linear with a negative slope when the reaction is
questions.explanation: [A] = [A]$_0 - kt$ is the equation of a straight line of slope $-k$.

questions.stem: A graph of $1/[\mathrm{A}]$ versus time is a straight line when the decay of A is
questions.explanation: The second-order integrated law is linear in $1/[\mathrm{A}]$, with slope $k$.

questions.stem: When a first-order reaction has consumed 75% of the reactant, the number of half-lives that have elapsed is
questions.explanation: 75% consumed means 25% remains, which is $(1/2)^2$ of the start, i.e. two half-lives.

questions.stem: Radioactive disintegration is treated kinetically as
options: first order in the amount of nuclide
second order in the daughter nuclide
third order in the neutron number
questions.explanation: Each nucleus decays independently, so the rate is proportional to the number remaining: first-order kinetics.

questions.stem: The half-life of a zero-order reaction with rate constant $k$ equals
questions.explanation: Set $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0/2$ in $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt$ to obtain $t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0/(2k)$.

questions.stem: A first-order process never quite reaches 100% conversion because
options: the rate keeps falling as [A] falls, so a finite time cannot exhaust the last traces
zero-order kinetics take over near the end
questions.explanation: [A] = [A]$_0 e^{-kt}$ approaches zero only as $t \to \infty$. In practice the reactant becomes undetectable, but the law has no finite finish time.

questions.stem: A first-order gas reaction has $k = 1.386 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$. Its half-life is
If 60% of a first-order reactant remains after 20 min, the leftover fraction after a further 20 min is nearest
questions.explanation: First order: the same time interval multiplies [A] by the same factor 0.60, so $0.60 \times 0.60 = 0.36$.

questions.stem: How long does a first-order reaction of half-life 15 min take to reach 75% completion?
questions.explanation: 75% completion is two half-lives, so $2 \times 15 = 30\ \mathrm{min}$.

questions.stem: From a measured first-order half-life of 46.2 min one obtains $k$ equal to
A zero-order reaction with $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ min^{-1}}$ and $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.20\ \mathrm{M}$ is complete after
questions.explanation: Completion means $[\mathrm{A}] = 0$, so $t = [\mathrm{A}]_0/k = 0.20/(2.0 \times 10^{-3}) = 100\ \mathrm{min}$.

questions.stem: Starting from a first-order sample, the number of half-lives needed to leave only one-eighth of the reactant is
For 2A → products, $k = 0.50\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}\ min^{-1}}$ and $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.20\ \mathrm{M}$. The half-life is
A first-order isomerisation has $t_{1/2} = 20\ \mathrm{min}$. The time required for 87.5% conversion is
questions.explanation: 87.5% converted leaves 12.5% = $1/8$, which is three half-lives: $3 \times 20 = 60\ \mathrm{min}$.

questions.stem: Half-life of a gaseous decay is 40 min at 0.80 bar initial pressure and 80 min at 0.40 bar. The order and $k$ (from the 0.80 bar run, treating concentration as proportional to $p$) are consistent with
options: second order, because $t_{1/2}$ doubles when $p_0$ is halved
first order, because $t_{1/2}$ is independent of $p_0$
zero order, because $t_{1/2}$ halves when $p_0$ is halved
questions.explanation: Second-order $t_{1/2} \propto 1/[\mathrm{A}]_0$. Halving the initial pressure doubles the half-life, which matches the data.

questions.stem: A first-order hydrolysis has $k = 2.303 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. The percentage of reactant still left after 1000 s is nearest
questions.explanation: $\log([\mathrm{A}]_0/[\mathrm{A}]) = kt/2.303 = 1.00$, so $[\mathrm{A}]/[\mathrm{A}]_0 = 0.10$ (10% remains).

questions.stem: Activation energy $E_a$ of a reaction is the
options: minimum extra energy that colliding molecules must possess if they are to react
same quantity as $\Delta H$ of the reaction
questions.explanation: $E_a$ is the barrier height on the reaction profile. Only collisions that clear that barrier can form products.

questions.stem: For a typical activated reaction, raising the temperature causes the rate constant to
options: become equal to the Faraday constant
questions.explanation: The Boltzmann factor $e^{-E_a/RT}$ grows as $T$ grows, so $k$ rises (often steeply).

questions.stem: A plot of $\ln k$ versus $1/T$ for an Arrhenius reaction is a straight line whose slope equals
questions.explanation: $\ln k = \ln A - E_a/RT$, so the slope versus $1/T$ is $-E_a/R$.

questions.stem: In $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$ the pre-exponential factor $A$ is interpreted as
options: a frequency (or collision) factor, the value $k$ would have if every collision were successful
questions.explanation: $A$ absorbs the collision frequency and a steric factor. It has the same units as $k$.

questions.stem: A catalyst speeds a reaction primarily by
options: providing an alternative path with a lower activation energy
raising the temperature of the surroundings
questions.explanation: A lower $E_a$ increases the fraction of successful collisions. $\Delta H$ and the position of equilibrium stay the same.

questions.stem: Threshold energy in collision theory is
options: the minimum relative kinetic energy that a collision must have to be potentially reactive
the average kinetic energy of the whole sample
the energy of the products minus $E_a$
questions.explanation: Molecules that meet with energy below the threshold simply bounce apart; those above it may react if oriented properly.

questions.stem: Activation energies of ordinary laboratory reactions are usually quoted in
questions.explanation: $E_a$ is a molar energy barrier, typically tens to a few hundred kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.stem: Between two reactions at the same $T$, the one with the larger $E_a$ is
options: more sensitive to a change of temperature
required to have a negative $A$ factor
questions.explanation: d ln $k$ / d$T$ = $E_a/RT^2$, so a higher barrier means a steeper rise of $k$ with $T$.

questions.stem: The two-temperature form of the Arrhenius equation is
questions.explanation: Subtracting $\ln k = \ln A - E_a/RT$ at two temperatures eliminates $A$ and gives that working equation.

questions.stem: In the formal high-temperature limit of the Arrhenius expression, $k$ approaches
questions.explanation: As $T \to \infty$, $e^{-E_a/RT} \to 1$, so $k \to A$. Real molecules decompose before that limit is reached.

questions.stem: A reaction has $k = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 300 K and $8.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 320 K. $E_a$ is nearest
If $E_a = 57.4\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$, the factor by which $k$ grows when $T$ goes from 300 K to 310 K is nearest
questions.explanation: $\log(k_2/k_1) = (57400/19.15)(10/93000) \approx 0.32$, so $k_2/k_1 \approx 2$. This is the familiar “about double per 10 K” case.

questions.stem: Given $k = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at 300 K and $E_a = 38.3\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$, $k$ at 310 K is nearest
On an Arrhenius plot of $\ln k$ versus $1/T$ the intercept (extrapolated to $1/T = 0$) equals
questions.explanation: $\ln k = \ln A - (E_a/R)(1/T)$. The intercept of that straight line is $\ln A$.

questions.stem: Two reactions have similar $A$ factors. At a given temperature the slower one is the one with
options: the larger $n$ in the Nernst equation
questions.explanation: $k = A e^{-E_a/RT}$ falls exponentially as $E_a$ rises, so the higher barrier is slower if $A$ is comparable.

questions.stem: From $k(300\ \mathrm{K}) = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $k(310\ \mathrm{K}) = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $k$ at 320 K is nearest
questions.explanation: First $E_a$ from the 300/310 pair ($k$ doubles in 10 K, $E_a \approx 53.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$), then $\log(k_{320}/k_{300}) \approx 0.58$, so $k_{320} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

questions.stem: Increasing the concentration of a reactant that appears in the rate law generally
questions.explanation: Rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]^x\ldots$ grows with [A] whenever the order $x$ is positive.

questions.stem: Heating a reaction mixture of thermally activated molecules typically
options: speeds the reaction because more molecules clear the energy barrier
always shifts the equilibrium constant to 1
questions.explanation: Temperature enters $k$ through the Arrhenius factor. Equilibrium may also shift, but that is a separate thermodynamic effect.

questions.stem: Adding a suitable catalyst to a reacting mixture
options: increases the rate by opening a lower-energy path
is consumed as a stoichiometric reactant
alters the value of $\Delta H$ for the net reaction
can change a first-order law into Faraday's law
questions.explanation: The catalyst is regenerated. It does not change the thermodynamics of the net reaction, only how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.stem: For a reaction between a solid and a gas or liquid, grinding the solid into a powder
options: raises the rate by exposing a larger surface
lowers the rate because grains are smaller
removes the need for a collision
questions.explanation: Heterogeneous rates scale with the available surface. A powder offers far more area than a single lump of equal mass.

questions.stem: Ionic reactions in water are often much faster than reactions of covalent organic molecules because
options: ions need little bond-breaking to meet, whereas covalent bonds must usually be broken and remade
questions.explanation: The nature of the reactants matters: many aqueous ion combinations are essentially encounter-controlled, unlike typical covalent substitutions.

questions.stem: Raising the pressure of a gaseous reactant (at fixed $T$) often increases the rate because
options: the concentration of that gas rises, and rate laws depend on concentration
questions.explanation: For an ideal gas, concentration $= p/RT$. A higher partial pressure therefore feeds the rate law.

questions.stem: Marble chips dissolve in acid more slowly than an equal mass of marble powder because the chips have
options: a smaller surface area available for collision with H$^+$
a larger $E^\circ$ as a galvanic anode
questions.explanation: The heterogeneous rate is surface-limited. Powdering increases the area and therefore the observed rate.

questions.stem: A catalyst that accelerates both the forward and reverse steps equally will
options: leave $\Delta H$ and the equilibrium constant unchanged
shift $K$ toward products at every temperature
questions.explanation: Equilibrium composition is fixed by $\Delta G^\circ$. The catalyst shortens the time needed to reach that same composition.

questions.stem: A photochemical reaction differs from an ordinary thermal reaction in that its rate
options: depends on the intensity (and wavelength) of the absorbed light
is completely independent of photon energy
can never involve a chain of radicals
questions.explanation: Absorption of a suitable photon supplies the activation; brighter light of the right colour produces more excited molecules per second.

questions.stem: A gas-phase reaction is first order in A. Doubling the partial pressure of A at constant $T$ and then raising $T$ so that $k$ also doubles will multiply the rate by
questions.explanation: First-order rate $= k[\mathrm{A}]$. Doubling [A] (via $p_A$) doubles the rate; doubling $k$ doubles it again, so the net factor is 4.

questions.stem: According to collision theory, a chemically effective encounter must supply at least the
options: standard EMF of a Daniell cell
questions.explanation: Only collisions whose relative kinetic energy exceeds $E_a$ can cross the barrier into products.

questions.stem: Besides enough energy, colliding molecules must also have a suitable
options: orientation of the reactive parts toward each other
questions.explanation: A steric (orientation) requirement means that a sideways or backside-wrong hit wastes the energy of an otherwise hot collision.

questions.stem: An effective collision is one that
options: has both sufficient energy and the correct geometry, and therefore leads to product
occurs at the wall of the vessel only
involves the solvent but never the solute
questions.explanation: Collision theory writes rate ∝ (collision frequency) × (energy factor) × (steric factor).

questions.stem: Most collisions in a gas-phase sample do not yield product because
options: they lack either the required energy or the required orientation (or both)
the collision frequency is exactly zero
Faraday's first law forbids gas reactions
questions.explanation: The exponential energy factor $e^{-E_a/RT}$ is usually ≪ 1, and the steric factor is also less than 1, so only a tiny fraction of hits succeed.

questions.stem: The steric factor $P$ introduced in collision theory is less than one when
options: only some geometries of an otherwise energetic collision can lead to reaction
questions.explanation: $P$ (also called the probability factor) corrects the simple hard-sphere collision rate for orientation and other restrictions.
